LHC will experience a substantial increase in luminosity, which will result in a significant rise in radiation levels. As a consequence, the LHC will face increased radiation damage to its beam instruments, particularly in detectors, which will compromise their functionality. To mitigate this issue, the LHC will adopt a more active strategy for protecting its detectors from radiation by employing various techniques, such as long-term monitoring, radiation monitoring during operation, and optimized calibration procedures. To support these efforts, the LHC Radiological Studies Working Group has been established to collect and analyze data on radiation levels in the detector areas. 

The purpose of this document is to present the Working Group's initial findings, which will inform future radiation studies and monitoring strategies. These studies are crucial for the development of radiation-hardened detectors and will help to establish reliable radiation monitoring systems, ultimately enabling the LHC to operate at higher luminosities in the coming years. 

This document will be regularly updated to incorporate the results of ongoing radiation studies and new data from the LHC. It will serve as a valuable resource for the LHC community, providing a platform for the exchange of ideas and the coordination of future radiation studies. 

The document will be supplemented by a comprehensive set of appendices, which will provide detailed information on the LHC beam instruments, the LHC detector areas, and the radiation monitoring equipment, as well as the current state of radiation studies and future prospects. 

The Working Group is actively seeking contributions from the LHC community, particularly in the areas of radiation monitoring, radiation studies, and long-term exposure. Your input is invaluable in helping to advance the LHC's radiation monitoring capabilities.

characteristics associated with each class of a multi-class classification model.

further divided into distinct "segmented profile" sections. Experimental results
demonstrate that this novel perspective offers valuable and practical insights
into the decision-making processes of neural networks, ultimately allowing for
improved transparency and model assessment. The accompanying code can be found

The simulation, conducted with the Gadget-4 code, employed a novel, self-interacting particle dark matter (SSS-SIMSDM) model that incorporates a realistic dark matter halo density profile.  The simulation achieved a high spatial resolution of $5$ pc after 100 million years of cosmic evolution.  The findings indicate that the fuzzy dark matter galaxy exhibits a distinct, diffuse stellar distribution, with a bright, central star cluster and a large, diffuse star-forming region.  The fuzzy dark matter model also predicts a unique, diffuse dark matter component that is concentrated at the galaxy's center, with a radius of approximately 1 kpc.  The researchers compared their results with observations of the Fuzzy Dark Matter galaxy F585, as well as with simulations of collisional invariants and a self-interacting dark matter model.  The findings suggest that the fuzzy dark matter model is a viable explanation for the observed properties of F585.  However, the researchers also identified some discrepancies between the simulation results and the observed data, particularly the lack of a distinct central galaxy component and the extended star-forming region.  The researchers proposed a possible method to distinguish between the fuzzy dark matter and collisional invariant models using observations of the galaxy's central density profile.  The researchers also highlighted the need for further, high-resolution simulations of fuzzy dark matter galaxies to better understand the impact of the SSS-SIMSDM model on the galaxy's structure.  The simulation data are publicly available on the Cornell Library website.  The researchers also provided a set of tools, referred to as the Fuzzy Dark Matter Galaxy Finder, to facilitate the identification of similar galaxies in large-scale surveys. This approach enables our method to be both more efficient and more effective in its use of camera information, resulting in superior segmentation capabilities. When tested on the challenging KITTI dataset, our method achieved performance levels comparable to previous state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conducted experiments to demonstrate the benefits of incorporating camera information in the construction of 3D point cloud representations, specifically highlighting the advantages of using hierarchical structures to process this information. In addition, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the impact of different camera information, such as color, depth, and infrared data, on our method's performance. Nevertheless, graphene inks' printing quality is compromised by graphene oxide defects and the presence of impurities and irregularity in the printing process. To address these issues, we developed an advanced transfer printing method that integrates mechanical pressing and ultrasonic vibration to achieve precise control over graphene printing precision. This method eliminates graphene printing defects, such as smudges and bubbles, and allows for printing at standard printing speeds. It also minimizes graphene thickness irregularities by reducing the impact of graphene surface irregularity and printing process defects. Additionally, we examined the influence of printing speed on graphene transfer quality and found that high-speed printing can be achieved with minimal irregularity. This method has the potential to improve the production of large, high-quality graphene printing and could be extended to printing other materials. Our approach builds on recent research in NLP by combining two techniques that
normally compete: high-dimensional linear transformations and power-law dimensionality
reductions, under the condition of sparse orthogonality. This allows us to train
our dictionaries on large collections of text, specifically the Wikipedia database,
and achieve state-of-the-art results in 17 languages using just 64 vectors. Our
method also demonstrates robust performance in classification tasks similar to
word identification, and it provides a valuable tool for exploring linguistic
concepts that are difficult to model using traditional methods. We also share our
trained embeddings and provide a user-friendly tool for exploratory data analysis
in 30 languages, along with a comprehensive set of visualizations. Our code and
data are freely available for download at the project's website, where users can
also upload their own vectors for analysis: https://wordvectorsexplainers.org.

Current methods, however, fail to accurately represent the complex, multi-dimensional relationships within light field data when calculating this cost. This paper introduces a novel light field matching cost framework based on a deep learning approach, incorporating multi-dimensional feature learning and a novel, multi-dimensional matching strategy. First, a light field feature extraction network is proposed, utilizing a multi-channel convolutional layer to capture the multi-dimensional, plenoptic data. Next, a cost volume-based module is designed to calculate the matching cost, a concept we term the multi-dimensional matching cost. Experimental results demonstrate that this new cost can more effectively capture the intricate, multi-view relationships within light field data and lead to improved results when used in conjunction with state-of-the-art cost volume filtering techniques. Furthermore, our research introduces a novel, multi-dimensional attention block, a component that has been shown to significantly enhance the light field depth estimation capabilities of cost volume filtering. This work provides valuable insights for future research into light field depth estimation using cost volume filtering.
